title: Pauli Error Composition Determines the Multipartite Advantage in Conference Key Agreement
authors: Ryder Carlson, Lochlan Fitzgerald, Kidus Peter, Wilson Smith
abstract: GHZ-based conference key agreement distributes a shared key to $N$ parties in one network use, whereas pairwise BB84 needs $N-1$. The survival of that advantage has been studied against party number, loss, and topology, but almost always with the channel fixed at depolarizing. Simulating both protocols exactly for $N = 3, 4, 5$ under dephasing, amplitude damping, and depolarizing noise, we find the crossover is set by the channel's Pauli error composition, not its identity: normalized to average infidelity, amplitude damping and depolarizing agree to within about 1\% at each group size, while dephasing can tolerate roughly $2.4\times$ more at $N = 3$.   We derive a closed-form rate for arbitrary per-party Pauli noise and use it to prove that concentrating a fixed noise budget on one arm is strictly worse than spreading it, and that giving the dealer role to the cleanest arm improves the rate by roughly 18\%. One structural fact drives every result: the phase-error term is a product over all $N$ arms, while the bit-error term stays local to a pair.
summary: This work analyzes the robustness of GHZ-based quantum key distribution against noise, showing the advantage over pairwise methods depends on the underlying Pauli error structure of the noise, not just its strength. Key findings include that noise should be spread evenly across all parties and that the dealer should be the party with the least noisy link. The study provides crucial theoretical bounds but notes that transmission loss remains the most significant physical omission.
main_problem: The paper investigates the conditions under which the multipartite advantage of GHZ-based conference key agreement over pairwise BB84 persists when subjected to various types of quantum noise.
main_result: The key advantage is determined by the channel's Pauli error composition, not its specific identity, and the rate is maximized by distributing noise evenly or assigning the dealer role to the cleanest party.
method: The authors simulate both protocols exactly for small $N$ under different noise channels and derive closed-form rate expressions for arbitrary Pauli noise.
model_or_system: The model uses quantum key distribution (QKD) protocols, specifically comparing GHZ-based conference key agreement against pairwise BB84 in a star network topology.
key_observables: Asymptotic conference key rates ($r_{GHZ}$) and pairwise key rates, measured via error rates like $Q_x$ (collective X error) and $Q_{1,i}$ (pairwise Z error).
important_parameters: Number of parties ($N=3, 4, 5$), noise types (Dephasing, Depolarizing, Amplitude Damping), and the distribution of a fixed total noise budget.
main_assumptions: The analysis assumes independent single-qubit channels on each arm and explicitly omits transmission loss, detector efficiency, and finite-key corrections.
figures_summary: Figure 1 illustrates the preparation and distribution of an N-qubit GHZ state, while tables compare key rates under different noise distribution strategies.
paper_structure: The paper establishes the theoretical framework by deriving closed-form rates for Pauli noise, compares the GHZ vs. pairwise protocols, analyzes the dependence on noise distribution (even vs. concentrated), and derives structural corollaries regarding the dealer role.
why_interesting: The finding that the advantage depends on the Pauli error composition rather than the channel type provides a powerful, general structural test for quantum communication protocols, applicable across different physical noise sources.
analysis_basis: full PDF text, analyzed in chunks

figures.caption: FIG. 2. Dephasing crossover threshold γ∗versus group size: closed form (line) against independent Cirq simulation (open squares), N = 3...5. The two bisections agree to 2.6 × 10−10, limited by the solver tolerance; the maximum pointwise key- rate discrepancy across 46 noise values and all three group sizes is 1.2 × 10−15.

FIG. 3. The GHZ–pairwise crossover at two noise compositions, N = 3. (a) Pure dephasing: the protocols cross at γ∗= 0.488. (b) Equal stacking of dephasing, amplitude damping, and depolarizing at a common strength: γ∗= 0.035, a factor of 14 lower. Note the tenfold difference in axis scale between panels, although the protocols and resource convention are identical.

FIG. 4. Crossover threshold γ∗as bit-flip-type error is ad- mixed into pure dephasing at ratio α (amplitude damping and depolarizing each at strength αγ), N = 3. All points share one parameterization, so thresholds are directly compa- rable. The collapse is front-loaded: 5% admixture more than halves the threshold, because it activates the h(Qz) term that pure dephasing leaves identically zero.

FIG. 5. Crossover thresholds versus group size for the three channels. (a) Raw parameter γ∗, which is not comparable across channels because Cirq parameterizes each independently. (b) The same thresholds normalized to average channel infidelity 1 −Favg: amplitude damping and depolarizing agree to within 1.2% at every N, while dephasing sits a factor of 2.4 to 2.1 higher. The channel ordering in (a) is an artifact of parameterization; the structure in (b) is physical.

FIG. 6. GHZ key rate under asymmetric dephasing on arms 1 and 2, with arm 3 noiseless, N = 3. The dashed line marks a fixed total budget γ1+γ2 = 0.6; along it the rate is maximized at the even split (star), the arithmetic–geometric-mean result proved in Section II G, and falls monotonically toward either concentrated end.
